newsitem.title: USA: NYC hopes to avoid inflating upstate land values.
newsitem.headline: NYC hopes to avoid inflating upstate land values.

text.p: New York City water officials on Thursday said they were confident that an agreement to spend up to $260 million to buy land upstate to protect the watershed would not let property owners jack up prices.

New York City's decision to buy the land at fair market value instead of taking it by using eminent domain was part of a watershed pact to protect the city's drinking water that it reached with upstate communities in early September.

The city now owns around 80,000 acres of the watershed, which extends 125 miles to its north and west, and it expects to buy about one-third of the 350,000 acres that it wants to protect. These sites include buffer areas around reservoirs, streams and wetlands.

New York City only has options on about 10,000 to 12,000 upstate acres and it has publicly identified which areas are the most critical. But New York City Municipal Water Finance Authority officials, who spoke at an investor conference it held, noted the watershed pact requires appraisels to be used, which will help ensure that prices do not skyrocket.

"As far as inviting some kind of chicanery, if you will, or changing of the numbers with a high-priority system, we really don't see that there's going to be much prospect of that because it is going to be all through a controlled appraisel," said Mark Hoffer, a utility official.

He predicted prices would only rise modestly. "There will probably be some inflative factor, if you will, attributable to the fact that we are a big buyer, that we are going to be out there actively solicting the land, but we don't think it'll be a major problem."

The safeguards also include the local communities' right to set aside some land, like town centres, which tends to be more costly than the vacant land the city wants. And New York City's experience shows that only about one in every three potential sellers is interested, so there will be a surplus of land, the officials said.
The watershed agreement, which the city hopes will allow it to avoid building a filtration system that could cost as much as $8 billion, is expected to be approved in November.

However, the city has not completely escaped the risk that the federal government will require it to build a filtration plant because it still has to find a way to protect the part of the water system in Putnam and Westchester counties.
Still, New York City Municipal Finance Water Authority officials appeared confident that the watershed agreement had made this problem more manageable.

Joel Miele, the commissioner of the authority, noted that only 45 days ago it appeared unlikely that Washington would signal its intention to waive until 2002 its filtration requirement for the western part of the watershed.
"Lo and behold, the immovable moved," he said. After 2002, authority officials hope that this mandate will be dropped for the part of the system covered by the watershed pact.
